messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 41
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Fast Food Worker
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 64

# Marcus

Marcus has worked the evening shift at the same fast-food restaurant for eight years. He knows the rhythm of the job—the dinner rush between five and seven, the late-night crowd after ten, the quiet hours in between when he can restock the freezer and clean the fryer. He's reliable, shows up on time, and the manager trusts him to close most nights. His regulars recognize him; some ask for his recommendations. It's honest work, and he's made peace with it.

Three months ago, everything changed. It was a Tuesday night, around nine o'clock. Marcus was at the register when a man came through the drive-through window—nothing unusual. But then the customer pulled a gun on the young cashier, a girl named Sophia who'd only been working there for two months. Marcus watched from the register as the man demanded cash. He remembers the exact tremor in Sophia's voice as she opened the drawer. He remembers the weight of his own paralysis, the way his hands seemed to belong to someone else. The police arrived within minutes, and the man fled. Sophia wasn't physically hurt, but she never came back to work after that night.

Now Marcus flinches at sounds—the beep of the register, a car backfiring in the parking lot, raised voices from customers. Last week, someone honked their horn at the drive-through speaker, and Marcus's hands shook so badly he had to step away from the counter. He's taken to standing with his back against the wall during his shift, positioning himself so he can see the entire restaurant. When customers raise their voices in frustration—about wait times or orders—his chest tightens and his breathing becomes shallow.

Sleep has become nearly impossible. Marcus lies awake replaying the scene, his mind cycling through variations of what could have happened. What if the man had fired? What if Sophia had tried to be a hero? He knows these thoughts are irrational, but knowing doesn't stop them. He's exhausted, moving through his days in a fog. On his days off, he stays home, avoiding the shopping center where the restaurant is located. Even driving past it makes his stomach clench.

He's withdrawn from the few friendships he maintained. His cousin called last week to invite him to a family dinner, and Marcus made an excuse. He didn't have the energy to explain what was wrong, and he didn't want to burden anyone with it. Besides, crowds feel dangerous now. He notices exits everywhere he goes. He watches people's hands. He categorizes threats.

The guilt is perhaps the heaviest part. Marcus feels ashamed that he froze, that he didn't do anything to help Sophia. Rationally, he knows that confronting an armed man would have been reckless, but the shame persists anyway. He also feels guilty that he still has his job, that he can still go to work, while Sophia is gone. Some nights he wonders if he should quit, if staying there is somehow disrespectful to what she experienced.

What troubles Marcus most is that he doesn't recognize himself anymore. He's always been someone who could handle things, who showed up and did what needed to be done. Now he's someone who jumps at sounds, who can't sleep, who avoids the world. The man with the gun is gone, arrested and out of his life. But the fear remains, taking up space in his chest, making his world smaller with each passing day.
